question_text: Choose the correctly spelled word to complete the sentence: 'Mr. Santos is the __ architect of the municipal urban plan.'

hint_ladder.title: What kind of word do we need here?
hint_ladder.text: Look at the word right after the blank: 'architect.' That's a noun, a person. So the missing word is describing that person — it's an adjective. Keep that in mind as you look at the options.

hint_ladder.title: The classic mix-up
hint_ladder.text: There are two words that sound almost the same but mean very different things. 'Principal' can mean 'most important' or 'head of a school.' 'Principle' always means a rule or a fundamental truth. Which one makes sense as an adjective describing an architect?

hint_ladder.title: Test each option in the sentence
hint_ladder.text: Read the sentence with each choice: 'Mr. Santos is the ___ architect.' Would you say 'the rule architect'? No. 'The most important architect'? Yes. That's your clue. Also, 'principaled' isn't a real word, and 'principles' is a plural noun — it can't describe a person.

hint_ladder.title: Almost there
hint_ladder.text: Only one option works as an adjective meaning 'primary' or 'lead.' It's the same word that describes the head of a school. The other options are either the wrong part of speech or not real words at all.

A.text: Correct! 'Principal' here is an adjective meaning 'most important' or 'primary.' It perfectly describes Mr. Santos as the lead architect of the plan. Great catch.

B.text: This is a very common mix-up. 'Principle' is always a noun that means a rule or a fundamental truth — like 'moral principles.' It can't describe an architect. The trap here is that both words sound identical, but their jobs in a sentence are completely different.

C.text: This isn't a real English word. It might look like it could work because we add '-ed' to some words to make adjectives, but 'principal' is already an adjective. No need to add anything. This is a case of overcorrecting.

D.text: 'Principles' is the plural form of 'principle,' meaning multiple rules. It's a noun, not an adjective, so it can't describe an architect. The trap here is thinking that adding an 's' might turn it into a describing word, but in English, plural nouns stay nouns.

next_time_rule: Here's a trick that will never fail you: 'Principal' ends with 'pal' — think of your school principal, who is your 'pal' and the head of the school. 'Principle' ends with 'ple' — think of 'rule.' If you can replace the word with 'main' or 'head,' use 'principal.' If you can replace it with 'rule,' use 'principle.'
deconstruct_text: Let's walk through this together. The sentence needs a word that describes Mr. Santos as an architect. That means we're looking for an adjective — a describing word. Now, among the options, only 'principal' can work as an adjective. It means 'most important' or 'primary,' which fits perfectly: Mr. Santos is the lead architect. 'Principle' is a noun that means a rule or truth — you wouldn't say 'the rule architect.' 'Principaled' isn't a real word at all. And 'principles' is just the plural of 'principle,' still a noun. So the only choice that makes sense both grammatically and in meaning is 'principal.' Here's a mental shortcut for next time: when you see a blank before a noun, ask yourself: 'Am I describing something or naming a rule?' If you're describing, go with 'principal.' If you're talking about a rule, it's 'principle.'
